title: Seven years, or seven days
hookLine: the promise: practice this way for seven years, or even seven days, and fruit comes (MN 10)
last: DHAMMAS — KNOW IT AS IT IS.

lines: THIRTY DAYS TO A NEW YOU.
cards: Gyms make promises. So do language apps and self-help books. Thirty days to a new you.
Fluent in three months. It's easy to get cynical about promises. So it's interesting that this old sutta, after all its careful instructions, ends with a promise of its own.
And the way it makes it is strange: it starts big and keeps getting smaller, lowering the bar on purpose. Today: seven years, or seven days.

teach.h: SEVEN YEARS: ONE OF TWO FRUITS.
teach.b: Here's how the Satipatthana Sutta ends. The Buddha says that if anyone should develop these four foundations in this way for seven years, one of two fruits can be expected. Either final knowledge, awakening, here and now.
Or, if some trace of clinging is left, the stage the tradition calls non-return. Then he stops himself. Never mind seven years.
Six years. Five. Four, three, two, one.
Never mind a year: seven months. Six months, down to one month, half a month. Never mind half a month.

teach.h: SIX, FIVE, FOUR, DOWN TO SEVEN DAYS.
teach.b: If anyone should develop these four foundations for seven days, one of these two fruits can be expected.
And then the sutta closes the circle with its opening line: this is the direct path, for the purification of beings. What do you do with a promise like that?
The tradition takes it seriously, and also knows the fruit depends on how deeply one practices, not only on the calendar.
The traditional commentary explains that the shorter times apply to people whose practice is already ripe. But any listener can take something from the countdown.

teach.h: A LOWERED BAR IS AN INVITATION.
teach.b: It's an invitation, not a threat. The Buddha doesn't say, this will take your whole life, so don't bother starting. He keeps lowering the bar until a person could actually step over it.
Seven days is not a lifetime. It's a week. You've already done more than thirty-seven of them on this path.

how: Insight meditation retreats in the Theravada world are often run as intensive practice for a set number of days, and some teachers cite the sutta's 'seven days' as encouragement.

games.q: the Buddha has just said 'seven years.' what does he say next?
o: 'never mind seven years': six, five, down to seven days.
games.why: he keeps lowering the time, down to seven days: an invitation to begin, not a wall.

practice: Rest with the breath for a moment. Then, if you'd like, pick one thing from these weeks, knowing the breath, naming your posture, catching the second arrow, naming a hindrance, and promise quietly: for seven days, I'll try this.
Let the promise settle, and simply sit with whatever is here.

wordCard.voice: Seven years. The sutta's closing promise: seven years, then fewer and fewer, down to even seven days of this practice, and fruit can be expected.

orig.note: Pali satta: seven, the number in the sutta's closing promise.

carryVoice: Your line: even seven days. The bar is low on purpose. That's day two hundred sixty-five.
